title: Notation
body_md: We denote by $\varepsilon>0$ the required accuracy in function value: the method must output a point $\hat x$ with $f(\hat x)-f^\ast\le\varepsilon$. The symbol $\|\cdot\|$ always stands for the Euclidean norm of a vector and the spectral norm of a matrix, $[x,y]$ is the segment with endpoints $x,y\in\mathbb R^d$, $B(x,r)$ is the closed ball of radius $r$ centered at $x$, and C--S stands for the Cauchy--Schwarz inequality. The sum of the first $k$ terms of a sequence is denoted by the corresponding capital letter: for example, $A_k=a_1+\dots+a_k$ and $A_0=0$.

label: prop:agm
title: \optim@proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:agm}
Let $L_1R\ge1$, and let the point $x'$ satisfy
\begin{align*}
 f(x')-f^\ast&\le\frac{L_0}{128L_1^2},\\
 \|x'-x^\ast\|&\le R .
\end{align*}
Then the points of Algorithm~\ref{alg:agm} satisfy, for all $k\ge1$,
\[
 f(y^k)-f^\ast\le\frac{18L_0R^2}{k^2} .
\]
In particular, for
\begin{equation}\label{eq:agm-N}
 N=\Bigl\lceil\sqrt{\frac{18L_0R^2}\varepsilon}\,\Bigr\rceil
\end{equation}
the algorithm finds a point with optimality gap at most $\varepsilon$ after at most
\[
 5\sqrt{\frac{L_0R^2}\varepsilon}+2
\]
oracle calls.
head: environment
name: Second stage

title: Proof
body_md:
This is Theorem~3.2 of \citet{tyurin2026accelerated} for $\ell(s)=L_0+L_1s$ with the accuracy parameter equal to twice the right-hand side of the first inequality of~\eqref{eq:stage-one-goal}. We verify its assumptions.
\begin{itemize}
\item The author of \citet{tyurin2026accelerated} states the result for twice differentiable functions, but notes (ibid., after Lemma~2.2) that instead of the Hessian bound the inequality
\[
 \|\nabla f(z)-\nabla f(y)\|\le\bigl(L_0+L_1\|\nabla f(y)\|\bigr)\frac{e^{L_1\|z-y\|}-1}{L_1}
\]
suffices. For our class this is Lemma~\ref{lem:gronwall}(b).
\item The function in the assumptions of Theorem~3.2 is strictly increasing on $[0,\infty)$, since for $t>0$
\[
 \frac{d}{dt}\,\frac{t^2}{2(L_0+4L_1t)}=\frac{t(L_0+2L_1t)}{(L_0+4L_1t)^2}>0 .
\]
\item The condition of Theorem~3.2 on the accuracy parameter holds with equality:
\[
 \ell\Bigl(8\sqrt{\ell(0)\,\frac{L_0}{64L_1^2}}\Bigr)=L_0+8L_1\sqrt{\frac{L_0^2}{64L_1^2}}=2L_0=2\ell(0) .
\]
\item In Theorem~3.2 the starting point of the accelerated method is obtained by gradient descent, but the proof (ibid., Appendix~E.1, formula~(32)) uses only its two properties~\eqref{eq:stage-one-goal}. For the point $x'$ they hold by assumption.
\item The number of preliminary iterations in Theorem~3.2 is zero:
\[
 \frac{\Gamma_0}{8L_0}=\frac1{512L_1^2R^2}\le\frac49 ,
\]
therefore
\[
 \max\Bigl\{1+\frac12\log_{3/2}\frac{\Gamma_0}{8L_0},\ 0\Bigr\}=0 .
\]
\end{itemize}
Theorem~3.2 gives the bound in the statement of the proposition. With $N$ chosen as in~\eqref{eq:agm-N}, its right-hand side for $k=N$ is at most $\varepsilon$. The algorithm computes gradients at the points $y^0,\dots,y^N$, so the number $N+1$ of its oracle calls satisfies
\[
 N+1\le\sqrt{\frac{18L_0R^2}\varepsilon}+2\le5\sqrt{\frac{L_0R^2}\varepsilon}+2 .
\]

label: lem:conj
title: \optim@lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:conj}
Let $K\subset\mathbb R^n$ be a nonempty convex compact set, let the function $H$ be continuous on $K$, and suppose that for all $z,z'\in K$ its restriction to the segment $[z,z']$ is strongly convex with modulus
\[
 \frac1{L_0+L_1\max\{\|z\|,\|z'\|\}} .
\]
Then for every $\sigma\in\mathbb R^n$ the function
\[
 \varphi(y)=\max_{z\in K}\bigl\{\langle y+\sigma,z\rangle-H(z)\bigr\}
\]
is convex and differentiable, its gradient $\nabla\varphi(y)$ is the unique maximizer $z(y)$, and for all $y,y'$
\begin{equation}\label{eq:conj-lip}
 \|\nabla\varphi(y)-\nabla\varphi(y')\|\le\Bigl(L_0+L_1\max\bigl\{\|\nabla\varphi(y)\|,\|\nabla\varphi(y')\|\bigr\}\Bigr)\|y-y'\| .
\end{equation}
In particular, $\varphi\in\mathcal F_{L_0,L_1}^n$.

label: prop:reduction
title: \optim@proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:reduction}
\leavevmode
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] Let $\varphi:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R$ be a convex chain, $d\ge2n$, and let every $d\times n$ matrix $V$ with orthonormal columns $v_1,\dots,v_n$ be assigned the function
\[
 F_V(x)=\varphi(V^\top x) .
\]
Suppose that every function $F_V$ attains its minimum and that for some $\mathrm{gap}>0$
\begin{equation}\label{eq:hidden-gap}
 \langle v_n,x\rangle=0\implies F_V(x)-\min F_V\ge\mathrm{gap}.
\end{equation}
Then for every deterministic method with $n-1$ oracle calls in $\mathbb R^d$ there exists $V$ such that $F_V(\hat x)-\min F_V\ge\mathrm{gap}$.
\item[(b)] Let a chain $\varphi\in\mathcal F_{L_0,L_1}^n$ have a minimizer of norm at most $R$, and let
\[
 \varphi(y)-\min\varphi\ge\mathrm{gap}>\varepsilon
\]
whenever $y_n=0$. Then $\mathcal N(\mathcal P_{\rm R})\ge n$. If, in addition, $\varphi(0)-\min\varphi\le\Delta$, then $\mathcal N(\mathcal P_\Delta)\ge n$.
\end{enumerate}

head: environment
name: Distance to the minimizer

title: Proof
body_md:
We bound the three quantities that make up the shifts $\sigma_i$:
\begin{align*}
 &2\log\Bigl(1+\frac{L_1G_1}{L_0}\Bigr)\mathrel{\underset{(\mathrm a)}{\le}}2\log\Bigl(1+\frac{L_1^2\varepsilon}{L_0}\Bigr)+2\sqrt{n\log(4n)},\\
 &4\log\bigl(1+\sqrt n\bigr)\mathrel{\underset{(\mathrm b)}{\le}}2\log(4n),\\
 &\sum_{k=i}^n\frac{G_k}{G_i}\mathrel{\underset{(\mathrm c)}{\le}}1+\sqrt{\frac n{\log(4n)}} .
\end{align*}
Here step (a) uses the inequality $\log(1+xe^v)\le\log(1+x)+v$ for $x,v\ge0$, step (b) uses the inequality $(1+\sqrt n)^2\le4n$, and step (c) uses the sum of a geometric progression together with the inequality $e^{-x}(1+x)\le1$. Adding these bounds, we obtain for every coordinate
\[
 L_1\sigma_i\le2\log\Bigl(1+\frac{L_1^2\varepsilon}{L_0}\Bigr)+4\sqrt{n\log(4n)}+2\log(4n)+2 .
\]
All $\sigma_i$ are positive, so $\|\sigma\|\le\sqrt n\max_i\sigma_i$ and
\[
 L_1\|\sigma\|\le2\sqrt n\log\Bigl(1+\frac{L_1^2\varepsilon}{L_0}\Bigr)+n\sqrt{\log(4n)}\,\Bigl[4+2\sqrt{\frac{\log(4n)}n}+\frac2{\sqrt{n\log(4n)}}\Bigr].
\]
The ratio of $\log(4n)$ to $n$ decreases and is therefore at most $\log4<2$, while $n\log(4n)\ge\log4>1$. Hence, the expression in brackets is less than $4+2\sqrt2+2<9$.

label: lem:choice
title: \optim@lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:choice}
If $L_0R^2\ge\varepsilon$ and $L_1R\ge16$, then
\[
 1+\mathcal N(\mathcal P_{\rm R})\ge\frac{L_1R}{24\sqrt{\log(2+L_1R)}} .
\]
head: environment
name: Choice of the chain length

title: Proof
body_md:
Set
\[
 n=\Bigl\lfloor\frac{L_1R}{24\sqrt{\log(2+L_1R)}}\Bigr\rfloor .
\]
If $n=0$, the statement is obvious. Let $n\ge1$. We verify condition~\eqref{eq:ordered-condition} by bounding its two terms.
\begin{itemize}
\item \emph{Second term.} The number $4n$ is less than $2+L_1R$, so $\log(4n)\le\log(2+L_1R)$ and
\[
 9n\sqrt{\log(4n)}\le9n\sqrt{\log(2+L_1R)}\mathrel{\underset{\text{def. of }n}{\le}}\frac38L_1R .
\]
\item \emph{First term.} The ratio of $\log^{3/2}(2+x)$ to $x$ decreases for $x\ge16$ and is less than three eighths at the point $16$. Therefore,
\begin{align*}
 2\sqrt n\log\Bigl(1+\frac{L_1^2\varepsilon}{L_0}\Bigr)
 &\mathrel{\underset{L_0R^2\ge\varepsilon}{\le}}2\sqrt n\log\bigl(1+(L_1R)^2\bigr)
 \mathrel{\underset{1+t^2\le(2+t)^2}{\le}}4\sqrt n\log(2+L_1R)\\
 &\mathrel{\underset{\text{def. of }n}{\le}}\frac4{\sqrt{24}}\,L_1R\,\sqrt{\frac{\log^{3/2}(2+L_1R)}{L_1R}}\\
 &\mathrel{\underset{L_1R\ge16}{<}}\frac4{\sqrt{24}}\sqrt{\frac38}\,L_1R=\frac{L_1R}2 .
\end{align*}
\end{itemize}
The sum of the terms is less than $L_1R$, and Theorem~\ref{thm:ordered} gives
\[
 1+\mathcal N(\mathcal P_{\rm R})\ge1+n\ge\frac{L_1R}{24\sqrt{\log(2+L_1R)}} .\qedhere
\]

name: Lower bound for the radius-only class

title: Proof
body_md:
We bound each of the three terms in brackets by $1+\mathcal N(\mathcal P_{\rm R})$.
\begin{itemize}
\item \emph{First.} Obviously, $1\le1+\mathcal N(\mathcal P_{\rm R})$.
\item \emph{Second.} Functions with $L_0$-Lipschitz gradient belong to the class. The classical bound \citep[Theorem~2.1.7]{nesterov2018lectures} together with Proposition~\ref{prop:reduction} gives
\[
 \sqrt{\frac{L_0R^2}\varepsilon}\le4\bigl(1+\mathcal N(\mathcal P_{\rm R})\bigr).
\]
\item \emph{Third.} For $L_1R\ge16$, by Lemma~\ref{lem:choice} it is at most $24(1+\mathcal N(\mathcal P_{\rm R}))$. For $L_1R<16$ it is less than $10$, since it increases in $L_1R$ and
\[
 \frac{16}{\sqrt{\log18}}\mathrel{\underset{\log18>4\log2}{<}}\frac{16}{\sqrt{4\log2}}\mathrel{\underset{\log2>2/3}{<}}\sqrt{96}<10 .
\]
\end{itemize}
Adding up, we obtain that the expression in brackets in~\eqref{eq:lower-radius} is at most $29(1+\mathcal N(\mathcal P_{\rm R}))$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
\leavevmode
\begin{itemize}
\item \emph{Necessity in~(a).} The gradient of a convex differentiable function is continuous \citep[Theorem~25.5]{rockafellar1970convex}, so on every ball it is bounded by some number $M$. If the segment $[x,y]$ lies in such a ball, then by~\eqref{eq:class}
\[
 \|\nabla f(x)-\nabla f(y)\|\le\ell(M)\|x-y\| .
\]
Hence, the map $t\mapsto\nabla f(x+tv)$ is Lipschitz on every segment, and therefore locally absolutely continuous and differentiable for almost all $t$. At such a point $t$, apply~\eqref{eq:class} to the points $x+tv$ and $x+(t+h)v$, divide by $|h|$ and let $h$ tend to zero. By the continuity of $\nabla f$ and $\ell$ we obtain~\eqref{eq:line-derivative}.
\item \emph{Sufficiency in~(a).} Let $v=y-x$. By the fundamental theorem of calculus and the monotonicity of $\ell$
\begin{align*}
 \|\nabla f(y)-\nabla f(x)\|
 &\le\int_0^1\ell\bigl(\|\nabla f(x+tv)\|\bigr)\|v\|\,dt\\
 &\le\ell\Bigl(\sup_{u\in[x,y]}\|\nabla f(u)\|\Bigr)\|x-y\| .
\end{align*}
\item \emph{Statement~(b).} For $f\in C^2$ the derivative of the map $t\mapsto\nabla f(x+tv)$ equals $\nabla^2f(x+tv)v$ and is continuous in $t$. Therefore, condition~\eqref{eq:line-derivative} for almost all $t$ is equivalent to the inequality
\[
 \|\nabla^2f(x)v\|\le\ell\bigl(\|\nabla f(x)\|\bigr)\|v\|
\]
for all $x$ and $v$. The Hessian of a convex $C^2$ function is a symmetric positive semidefinite matrix, and for it this inequality is equivalent to~\eqref{eq:hessian-bound}. It remains to apply~(a).\qedhere
\end{itemize}

title: Proof

head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
For $\nabla f(y)=0$ the statement coincides with the convexity inequality. Let $\nabla f(y)\ne0$. We compare the affine approximation at $y$ with the growth bound of Lemma~\ref{lem:radial} at the points of the ray
\[
 z_t=x^\ast+\frac{t\,\nabla f(y)}{\|\nabla f(y)\|},
\]
where $t\ge0$.
\begin{itemize}
\item \emph{Bound for fixed $t$.} Since $\langle \nabla f(y),z_t-x^\ast\rangle=t\|\nabla f(y)\|$,
\begin{align*}
 f(y)+\langle \nabla f(y),x^\ast-y\rangle+t\|\nabla f(y)\|
 &\mathrel{\underset{\mathmakebox[\widthof{$\scriptstyle(\mathrm a)$}]{}}{=}}f(y)+\langle \nabla f(y),z_t-y\rangle\\
 &\mathrel{\underset{(\mathrm a)}{\le}}f(z_t)
 \mathrel{\underset{(\mathrm b)}{\le}}f^\ast+\frac{L_0}{L_1^2}\bigl(e^{L_1t}-1-L_1t\bigr),
\end{align*}
where step (a) uses convexity and step (b) uses Lemma~\ref{lem:radial}.
\item \emph{Choice of $t$.} Set
\[
 t=\frac1{L_1}\log\Bigl(1+\frac{L_1\|\nabla f(y)\|}{L_0}\Bigr).
\]
Then
\[
 e^{L_1t}=1+\frac{L_1\|\nabla f(y)\|}{L_0},
\]
and a direct computation using formula~\eqref{eq:Phi} gives
\[
 t\|\nabla f(y)\|-\frac{L_0}{L_1^2}\bigl(e^{L_1t}-1-L_1t\bigr)=\Phi\bigl(\|\nabla f(y)\|\bigr).
\]
Substituting this into the previous bound, we obtain the statement of the lemma.\qedhere
\end{itemize}
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Denote by $z(t)=v+t(x-v)$ the points of the segment $[v,x]$. The function $t\mapsto f(z(t))$ is convex on $[0,1]$, and its derivative $\langle \nabla f(z(t)),x-v\rangle$ is nondecreasing. For the point $y=z(t)$
\[
 \langle \nabla f(y),y-v\rangle=t\,\langle \nabla f(z(t)),x-v\rangle .
\]
\begin{itemize}
\item \emph{Stopping criterion.} If it was triggered at a point $z\in[v,x]$, then $z$ lies in the ball $B(x^\ast,r)$, and by convexity
\[
 f(z)-f^\ast\le\langle \nabla f(z),z-x^\ast\rangle\le r\|\nabla f(z)\|\le\delta .
\]
From now on we assume that the stopping criterion was not triggered.
\item \emph{Return at the endpoints of the segment.} If $\langle \nabla f(v),x-v\rangle\ge0$, then the derivative is nonnegative on $[0,1]$. Hence, $f(v)\le f(x)$, and for $y=v$ the left-hand side of the second inequality of~\eqref{eq:search} is zero. If $\langle \nabla f(x),x-v\rangle\le0$, then for $y=x$ the first inequality of~\eqref{eq:search} is obvious, and the left-hand side of the second one is nonpositive.
\item \emph{Bisection.} The algorithm maintains the inequalities
\[
 \langle \nabla f(z(t_-)),x-v\rangle<0<\langle \nabla f(z(t_+)),x-v\rangle .
\]
If the derivative at the midpoint is zero, then this midpoint minimizes the function on the segment, and both inequalities~\eqref{eq:search} hold for it. Otherwise, after $m$ steps $t_+-t_-=2^{-m}$.
\item \emph{Decrease for $y=z(t_+)$.} The derivative at the point $t_+$ is positive, so the function is nondecreasing on $[t_+,1]$, and $f(y)\le f(x)$.
\item \emph{Error for $y=z(t_+)$.} The distance between the points $z(t_+)$ and $z(t_-)$ equals $2^{-m}\|x-v\|$, and $\|x-v\|\le2r$. By condition~\eqref{eq:search-m}
\[
 L_1\|z(t_+)-z(t_-)\|\le2^{1-m}L_1r\le\frac{2L_1r}{128\bigl(1+L_1r\bigr)^2}\le\frac1{32} .
\]
By Lemma~\ref{lem:gronwall}(b) with base point $z(t_+)$ and the inequality $e^s-1\le se^s$
\[
 \|\nabla f(z(t_+))-\nabla f(z(t_-))\|\le2\bigl(L_0+L_1\|\nabla f(y)\|\bigr)\|z(t_+)-z(t_-)\| .
\]
Since $\langle \nabla f(z(t_-)),x-v\rangle<0$ and $t_+\le1$,
\begin{align*}
 \langle \nabla f(y),y-v\rangle
 &\mathrel{\underset{\mathmakebox[\widthof{$\scriptstyle\eqref{eq:search-m}$}]{}}{\le}}t_+\langle \nabla f(z(t_+))-\nabla f(z(t_-)),x-v\rangle\\
 &\mathrel{\underset{\mathmakebox[\widthof{$\scriptstyle\eqref{eq:search-m}$}]{(\mathrm a)}}{\le}}2r\|\nabla f(z(t_+))-\nabla f(z(t_-))\|\\
 &\mathrel{\underset{\mathmakebox[\widthof{$\scriptstyle\eqref{eq:search-m}$}]{}}{\le}}2^{3-m}r^2\bigl(L_0+L_1\|\nabla f(y)\|\bigr)\\
 &\mathrel{\underset{\eqref{eq:search-m}}{\le}}\frac{r^2\bigl(L_0+L_1\|\nabla f(y)\|\bigr)}{16\bigl(1+L_0r^2/\delta+L_1r\bigr)^2} ,
\end{align*}
where step (a) uses the inequalities $t_+\le1$ and $\|x-v\|\le2r$.
\item \emph{Relation to the gradient.} The stopping criterion does not hold at $y$, that is, $r\|\nabla f(y)\|>\delta$. Therefore,
\begin{align*}
 \frac{r\bigl(L_0+L_1\|\nabla f(y)\|\bigr)}{\|\nabla f(y)\|}
 &\mathrel{\underset{\mathmakebox[\widthof{$\scriptstyle(\mathrm b)$}]{}}{=}}\frac{L_0r}{\|\nabla f(y)\|}+L_1r\\
 &\mathrel{\underset{(\mathrm b)}{<}}\frac{L_0r^2}\delta+L_1r
 <1+\frac{L_0r^2}\delta+L_1r ,
\end{align*}
where step (b) uses the inequality $r\|\nabla f(y)\|>\delta$. Squaring and dividing by $16(L_0+L_1\|\nabla f(y)\|)$, we obtain
\[
 \frac{r^2\bigl(L_0+L_1\|\nabla f(y)\|\bigr)}{16\bigl(1+L_0r^2/\delta+L_1r\bigr)^2}<\frac{\|\nabla f(y)\|^2}{16\bigl(L_0+L_1\|\nabla f(y)\|\bigr)} ,
\]
and the second inequality of~\eqref{eq:search} holds.
\item \emph{Number of calls.} The algorithm makes two calls at the endpoints of the segment and at most $m$ calls at midpoints.\qedhere
\end{itemize}

body_md:
\label{lem:eq-chain}
The function $\psi$ is convex, continuously differentiable, and
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] its minimum is zero, and the set of minimizers is
\[
 \bigl\{y\in\mathbb R^n:\ y_i\le-(\sigma_i+b)\ \text{for}\ i=1,\dots,n\bigr\}.
\]
The minimizer closest to zero, $-b\,(2n,2n-1,\dots,n+1)$, has norm $R$,
\item[(b)] $\psi(0)=(4-2/n)\varepsilon$,
\item[(c)] $\psi(y)\ge2\varepsilon$ whenever $y_n=0$,
\item[(d)] $\psi$ is a chain,
\item[(e)] $\nabla\psi(y)=z(y)=G\,(p_1,\dots,p_n)$, where $z(y)$ is the unique maximizer in~\eqref{eq:eq-chain}.
\end{enumerate}

name: Properties of the chain with equal slopes

label: eq:eq-kkt
title: Proof
body_md:
\leavevmode
\begin{itemize}
\item \emph{Gradient.} The strong convexity of $r$ gives the strong convexity of $H$ on $K$ with a constant modulus. Therefore, the maximizer is unique and, as in the proof of Lemma~\ref{lem:conj}, $\nabla\psi(y)=z(y)$ and the gradient is continuous. This is statement~(e).
\item \emph{Optimality conditions.} Set $\theta_0=0$ and $\theta_i=y_i+\sigma_i$ for $i\ge1$. The maximization problem in~\eqref{eq:eq-chain} is equivalent to maximizing
\[
 \sum_{i=0}^n\theta_ip_i-\sum_{i=0}^nr(p_i)
\]
over the simplex. Moving weight between two positive coordinates and from a positive coordinate to a zero one gives a number $\nu$ such that for $0\le i\le n$
\begin{equation}\label{eq:eq-kkt}
 \theta_i\ \begin{cases}=\nu+r'(p_i), & p_i>0,\\ \le\nu, & p_i=0.\end{cases}
\end{equation}
These conditions are also sufficient by the convexity of $r$. Since $0\le r'(p_i)\le b$, we always have $\nu\ge\theta_i-b$.
\item \emph{Statement~(a).} The point $z=0$ is feasible, so $\psi\ge0$. Equality holds exactly when the vector $p=e_0$ is optimal. By~\eqref{eq:eq-kkt} this is equivalent to $\nu=-b$ and $\theta_i\le-b$ for $i\ge1$. The formulas for the set of minimizers and the minimizer closest to zero follow from~\eqref{eq:eq-chain-params}.
\item \emph{Statement~(b).} For $y=0$, conditions~\eqref{eq:eq-kkt} hold for $p=e_1$ and $\nu=\sigma_1-b=(2n-2)b$: all other $\theta_i$, including $\theta_0=0$, are at most $\nu$. Therefore, $\psi(0)=G\sigma_1=(4-2/n)\varepsilon$.
\item \emph{Statement~(c).} Substituting $z=Ge_n$, we obtain $\psi(y)\ge G\sigma_n=2\varepsilon$.
\item \emph{Statement~(d).} If $y_i=0$ for $i\ge j$, then for $l>j$
\[
 \theta_l=\sigma_l\le\sigma_j-b=\theta_j-b\le\nu .
\]
A positive $p_l$ would contradict~\eqref{eq:eq-kkt}, since $r'(p_l)>0$. Hence, the $l$-th coordinate of the gradient $Gp_l$ is zero.\qedhere
\end{itemize}

title: Proof
body_md:
The proof repeats the proof of Lemma~\ref{lem:energy}. For $k=0$, inequality~\eqref{eq:energy-gap} follows from the conditions on $x^0$. The induction step differs in three places.
\begin{itemize}
\item \emph{Replacements.} Instead of Lemma~\ref{lem:anchored}, the convexity inequality $\langle \nabla f(y^k),y^k-x^\ast\rangle\ge f(y^k)-f^\ast$ is used, and Lemma~\ref{lem:search} is used in the same way. Inequalities~\eqref{eq:gap-monotone} follow from it and Lemma~\ref{lem:safe-step}.
\item \emph{Increment.} With these replacements, the bounds on the distance and on the optimality gap from the proof of Lemma~\ref{lem:energy} give
\begin{align*}
 \MoveEqLeft\Bigl[A_k\bigl(f(x^k)-f^\ast\bigr)+\frac12\|v^k-x^\ast\|^2\Bigr]-\Bigl[A_{k-1}\bigl(f(x^{k-1})-f^\ast\bigr)+\frac12\|v^{k-1}-x^\ast\|^2\Bigr]\\
 &\mathrel{\underset{\mathmakebox[\widthof{$\scriptstyle\eqref{eq:coef-gap-rule}$}]{}}{\le}}\Bigl(\frac{a_k}{16}-\frac{5A_k}{24}\Bigr)\frac{\|\nabla f(y^k)\|^2}{L_0+L_1\|\nabla f(y^k)\|}+\frac12a_k^2\|\nabla f(y^k)\|^2\\
 &\mathrel{\underset{\eqref{eq:coef-gap-rule}}{=}}\Bigl(\frac{a_k}{16}-\frac{5A_k}{24}+\frac{A_k}{32}\Bigr)\frac{\|\nabla f(y^k)\|^2}{L_0+L_1\|\nabla f(y^k)\|}-\frac12a_k^2\|\nabla f(y^k)\|^2\\
 &\mathrel{\underset{\mathmakebox[\widthof{$\scriptstyle\eqref{eq:coef-gap-rule}$}]{(\mathrm a)}}{\le}}-\frac12a_k^2\|\nabla f(y^k)\|^2 ,
\end{align*}
where step (a) uses the inequalities $a_k\le A_k$ and $1/16-5/24+1/32<0$.
\item \emph{Ball of radius $r$.} By inequality~\eqref{eq:energy-gap} and the assumption of the lemma
\[
 \|v^k-x^\ast\|^2\le R_0^2+2a_0\Delta_0\le r^2 ,
\]
and the point $x^k$ lies in the ball by Lemma~\ref{lem:safe-step}.\qedhere
\end{itemize}

label: lem:block
title: \optim@lemma
head: environment
name: Block bound

label: eq:block-g
title: Proof
body_md:
All sums in the proof are over $i=k+1,\dots,k+N$.
\begin{itemize}
\item \emph{Optimality gap through the weights.} We have
\begin{align*}
 f(x^{k+N})-f^\ast
 &\mathrel{\underset{\eqref{eq:energy-gap}}{\le}}\frac{R^2}{2A_{k+N}}
 \le\frac{R^2}{2\bigl(\sqrt{A_{k+N}}-\sqrt{A_k}\bigr)^2}\\
 &\mathrel{\underset{\eqref{eq:coef-gap}}{\le}}\frac{64R^2}{\Bigl(\sum_i\bigl(L_0+L_1\|\nabla f(y^i)\|\bigr)^{-1/2}\Bigr)^2} .
\end{align*}
\item \emph{Hölder's inequality.} With exponents $3/2$ and $3$
\begin{align*}
 N&=\sum_i\bigl(L_0+L_1\|\nabla f(y^i)\|\bigr)^{-1/3}\bigl(L_0+L_1\|\nabla f(y^i)\|\bigr)^{1/3}\\
 &\le\Bigl(\sum_i\bigl(L_0+L_1\|\nabla f(y^i)\|\bigr)^{-1/2}\Bigr)^{2/3}\Bigl(\sum_i\bigl(L_0+L_1\|\nabla f(y^i)\|\bigr)\Bigr)^{1/3} .
\end{align*}
Substituting into the previous bound, we obtain
\begin{equation}\label{eq:block-g}
\begin{aligned}
 f(x^{k+N})-f^\ast
 &\le\frac{64R^2}{N^3}\sum_i\bigl(L_0+L_1\|\nabla f(y^i)\|\bigr)\\
 &=\frac{64L_0R^2}{N^2}+\frac{64L_1R^2}{N^3}\sum_i\|\nabla f(y^i)\| .
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
\item \emph{The sum of gradient norms is small when the optimality gap is small.} Summing inequalities~\eqref{eq:gap-monotone} over the block, we obtain
\[
 \sum_i\frac{\|\nabla f(y^i)\|^2}{L_0+L_1\|\nabla f(y^i)\|}\le8\bigl(f(x^k)-f^\ast\bigr).
\]
By the Cauchy--Schwarz inequality
\begin{align*}
 \Bigl(\sum_i\|\nabla f(y^i)\|\Bigr)^2
 &\le\sum_i\frac{\|\nabla f(y^i)\|^2}{L_0+L_1\|\nabla f(y^i)\|}\cdot\sum_i\bigl(L_0+L_1\|\nabla f(y^i)\|\bigr)\\
 &\le8\bigl(f(x^k)-f^\ast\bigr)\Bigl(NL_0+L_1\sum_i\|\nabla f(y^i)\|\Bigr).
\end{align*}
If the sum $\sum_i\|\nabla f(y^i)\|$ exceeded $\sqrt{8NL_0(f(x^k)-f^\ast)}+8L_1(f(x^k)-f^\ast)$, then its square would exceed this quantity times the sum itself, which is at least the right-hand side of the last inequality. Therefore,
\[
 \sum_i\|\nabla f(y^i)\|\le\sqrt{8NL_0\bigl(f(x^k)-f^\ast\bigr)}+8L_1\bigl(f(x^k)-f^\ast\bigr).
\]
\item \emph{Substitution.} Substitute this bound into~\eqref{eq:block-g}. The second term in~\eqref{eq:block-g} becomes at most
\[
 \frac{64L_1R^2}{N^3}\sqrt{8NL_0\bigl(f(x^k)-f^\ast\bigr)}+\frac{512\,L_1^2R^2\bigl(f(x^k)-f^\ast\bigr)}{N^3} .
\]
By the inequality between the arithmetic and geometric means, the first of these terms is at most
\[
 \frac{32L_0R^2}{N^2}+\frac{256\,L_1^2R^2\bigl(f(x^k)-f^\ast\bigr)}{N^3} .
\]
Therefore,
\[
 f(x^{k+N})-f^\ast\le\frac{96L_0R^2}{N^2}+\frac{768\,L_1^2R^2\bigl(f(x^k)-f^\ast\bigr)}{N^3} .
\]
Since $768\le3072$, we obtain~\eqref{eq:block}.\qedhere
\end{itemize}

label: thm:upper-gap
title: \optim@theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:upper-gap}
Let $f\in\mathcal F_{L_0,L_1}^d$, $\|x^0-x^\ast\|\le R$ and $\varepsilon>0$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] If $f(x^0)-f^\ast\le4\varepsilon$, then Algorithm~\ref{alg:am-gap} with $a_0=0$, $r=R$, $\delta=\varepsilon$,
\[
 m=\Bigl\lceil\log_2\Bigl(128\Bigl(1+\frac{L_0R^2}\varepsilon+L_1R\Bigr)^2\Bigr)\Bigr\rceil
\]
and the number of iterations
\begin{align*}
 K&=\max\Bigl\{1,\Bigl\lceil\sqrt{\frac{192L_0R^2}\varepsilon}\,\Bigr\rceil,\bigl\lceil(24576\,L_1^2R^2)^{1/3}\bigr\rceil\Bigr\}\\
 &\le3+14\sqrt{\frac{L_0R^2}\varepsilon}+30(L_1R)^{2/3}
\end{align*}
outputs a point with optimality gap at most $\varepsilon$ after at most $K(m+2)$ oracle calls.
\item[(b)] If a number $\Delta>\varepsilon$ with $f(x^0)-f^\ast\le\Delta$ is known, then Algorithm~\ref{alg:am-gap} with parameters~\eqref{eq:weight-params},
\[
 m=\Bigl\lceil\log_2\Bigl(128\Bigl(1+\frac{2L_0R^2}\varepsilon+\sqrt2L_1R\Bigr)^2\Bigr)\Bigr\rceil
\]
and the number of iterations
\[
 K=\Bigl\lceil16\sqrt{\frac{L_0R^2}\varepsilon}+21\,(L_1R)^{2/3}\log^{2/3}\frac{2\Delta}\varepsilon\Bigr\rceil
\]
outputs such a point after at most $K(m+2)$ oracle calls. For $\Delta\le\varepsilon$ it suffices to return $x^0$.
\end{enumerate}
In both cases the method uses only gradients and does not use the value $f^\ast$. In case~(a) it does not use a bound on the initial optimality gap either.

\begin{itemize}
\item \emph{Part~(a).} If the stopping criterion was triggered, the output is correct by Lemma~\ref{lem:search}. Otherwise bound~\eqref{eq:block} with $k=0$ and $f(x^0)-f^\ast\le4\varepsilon$ gives
\[
 f(x^K)-f^\ast\le\frac{96L_0R^2}{K^2}+\frac{3072\,L_1^2R^2\cdot4\varepsilon}{K^3}\mathrel{\underset{(\mathrm a)}{\le}}\frac\varepsilon2+\frac\varepsilon2 ,

where step (a) uses the choice of $K$. The bound on $K$ follows from the inequalities $\sqrt{192}<14$ and $24576^{1/3}<30$.
\item \emph{Part~(b).} For $\Delta\le\varepsilon$ we return $x^0$. Otherwise, by Lemma~\ref{lem:count-weight}, after $K$ iterations either the stopping criterion was triggered and the output is correct by Lemma~\ref{lem:search}, or $f(x^K)-f^\ast\le\varepsilon$.
\end{itemize}
In both parts the number of calls is at most $K(m+2)$.

label: prop:fixed-dim
title: \optim@proposition
head: environment
name: Center-of-gravity method

label: eq:fixed-envelope
title: Proof
body_md:
\leavevmode
\begin{itemize}
\item \emph{Ball of points with small optimality gap.} By Lemma~\ref{lem:radial}, for every $x$
\begin{equation}\label{eq:fixed-envelope}
 f(x)-f^\ast\le\frac{L_0}{L_1^2}\bigl(e^{L_1\|x-x^\ast\|}-1-L_1\|x-x^\ast\|\bigr).
\end{equation}
Consequently, in the ball $B(x^\ast,\min\{R,\rho_\varepsilon\})$ the optimality gap is at most $\varepsilon$.
\item \emph{Center-of-gravity method.} Without loss of generality $x^0=0$. Start with the cube $K_0=[-2R,2R]^d$. It contains the ball $B(x^\ast,\min\{R,\rho_\varepsilon\})$, since $\|x^\ast\|\le R$. At step $k$, compute the center of gravity $c_k$ of the polytope $K_{k-1}$ and call the oracle at this point. If $\nabla f(c_k)=0$, then $c_k$ is a minimizer. Otherwise set
\[
 K_k=K_{k-1}\cap\bigl\{z:\ \langle \nabla f(c_k),z-c_k\rangle\le0\bigr\}.
\]
After the prescribed number of steps, return the query point with the smallest function value. Computing the centers of gravity between oracle calls is not counted.
\item \emph{The ball is preserved.} Suppose that at all of the first $N$ query points the optimality gap exceeds $\varepsilon$. For every point $z$ of the ball $B(x^\ast,\min\{R,\rho_\varepsilon\})$, convexity and~\eqref{eq:fixed-envelope} give
\[
 \langle \nabla f(c_k),z-c_k\rangle\le f(z)-f(c_k)<0 .
\]
Hence, the whole ball is preserved after each cut.
\item \emph{Comparison of volumes.} By Grünbaum's theorem \citep{grunbaum1960partitions}, every hyperplane through the center of gravity of a convex body leaves in each of the two half-spaces at least $1/e$ of its volume. The unit ball contains the cube $[-1/\sqrt d,1/\sqrt d]^d$, so its volume is at least $(2/\sqrt d)^d$. Consequently,
\begin{align*}
 \Bigl(\frac{2\min\{R,\rho_\varepsilon\}}{\sqrt d}\Bigr)^d
 &\mathrel{\underset{(\mathrm a)}{\le}}\operatorname{vol}(K_N)\\
 &\mathrel{\underset{(\mathrm b)}{\le}}\Bigl(1-\frac1e\Bigr)^N(4R)^d ,
\end{align*}
where step (a) uses the preservation of the ball and step (b) uses Grünbaum's theorem.
For $N$ equal to~\eqref{eq:centroid-count}, the right-hand side is strictly smaller than the left-hand side. This contradiction shows that at least one of the query points has optimality gap at most $\varepsilon$.
\item \emph{One-dimensional case.} Start with the segment $[-R,R]$. At each step, call the oracle at the midpoint of the current segment. If the derivative there is positive, keep the left half, if it is negative, keep the right half, and if it is zero, an exact minimizer has been found. The monotonicity of the derivative of a convex function guarantees that the minimizer stays in the segment. After $n$ calls, the midpoint $\hat x$ of the remaining segment satisfies
\begin{align*}
 |\hat x-x^\ast|&\mathrel{\underset{\mathmakebox[\widthof{$\scriptstyle\eqref{eq:fixed-envelope}$}]{}}{\le}}R\,2^{-n},\\
 f(\hat x)-f^\ast&\mathrel{\underset{\eqref{eq:fixed-envelope}}{\le}}\frac{L_0}{L_1^2}\bigl(e^{L_1R2^{-n}}-1-L_1R\,2^{-n}\bigr).
\end{align*}
For $n$ equal to~\eqref{eq:one-dim-count}, we have $R2^{-n}\le\rho_\varepsilon$, and the right-hand side is at most $\varepsilon$. The oracle may not have been called at the output midpoint. If the output must coincide with a query point, one more call is needed.\qedhere
\end{itemize}
head: environment

label: rem:fixed-dim-growth
title: \optim@remark
body_md:
\label{rem:fixed-dim-growth}
For fixed $d$ and $L_1^2\varepsilon/L_0$, Proposition~\ref{prop:fixed-dim} gives only $O(\log(2+L_1R))$ calls. Therefore, a lower bound that is linear in $L_1R$ up to logarithms cannot be realized by a family of fixed dimension. It requires a mechanism that hides information in a number of directions growing together with the number of calls. This is exactly why Theorems~\ref{thm:lower-gap} and~\ref{thm:lower-radius} use a dimension proportional to the chain length.
